Wildfire structure loss

Wildfire building loss: highlights so far · 2026-10-18

A short tour, for discussion, of the clearest results from the U.S. wildfire building-loss work: losses over time, how we defined an urban conflagration, when a wildfire becomes one, what puts a building at risk inside a fire, and what the extended record adds. Each panel links to the page with the full analysis.

By Carlo Broderick, NCEAS, UC Santa Barbara · 2026-10-18 19:56 PDT

Not exhaustive: a selection to start a conversation. Each panel has its own Plain / Technical switch; hover or tap any bar, line or heading for the numbers behind it.

In brief

  • Losses are rising, and the rise is in the worst fires. Buildings destroyed per year rose ×3.3 between 2008-2016 and 2017-2025 in the national situation reports, while the number of fires that destroyed any building barely moved (×1.06); a few disaster years carry much of the rise. The worst 1% of loss fires hold 34–51% of all destroyed buildings.
  • We propose a countable definition of an urban conflagration: a patch of at least 50 destroyed buildings, each within 30 m of another. The data do not pick these numbers (there is no natural size, and clustering builds between about 20 and 50 m), so they are stated as conventions; no other candidate matched published accounts of named fires better.
  • A town fire needs a big block of close houses. No fire whose largest block held 89 buildings or fewer became an urban conflagration (0 of 338, 714 and 429 fires in the three records), but tested, that is mostly because almost no smaller town could hold one. Every one in our records burned in a wind event, which was not automatic (about one ordinary day in five qualifies); Waldo Canyon 2012, outside the records, did not. In big blocks, losses spread house to house far more, yet the wind direction does not pick which neighbour burns next (no downwind lean larger than about 2 points).
  • Inside a fire, mobile homes are lost more often than houses; whether crowded buildings are lost more often depends mostly on a handful of very large fires.
  • Picking fires by their losses, as most studies do, makes a typical fire look 2 to 3 times as destructive, and today's building maps have already lost many of the buildings older fires destroyed.

The three records used throughout

  • Carlson 2002–22: USGS hand-mapped buildings for every fire that destroyed 10 or more.
  • Our 2002–26 record: Carlson plus the 2023–26 fires our satellite pipeline mapped, using CAL FIRE's inspection outcome wherever a building was inspected.
  • CAL FIRE DINS 2013–25: CAL FIRE's door-to-door damage inspections, every incident on file.

Where a fire's outline matters, every panel uses the Forest Service / USGS burned-area outline (MTBS) plus 100 m.

1 · Losses are rising, and the rise is in the worst fires

Every record shows more buildings lost per year. A few fires carry most of the loss, and the growth comes from those fires getting worse, not from more fires destroying a few houses each. A handful of disaster years drive much of it, so the size of the rise is uncertain; its direction is not.

Each bar is the share of a record's destroyed buildings that its most destructive 1%, 5% or 10% of fires hold. 2 · Defining an urban conflagration: what we propose and how we got there

Published accounts describe urban conflagrations in words; none gives a rule that can be counted on a map of destroyed buildings. We built one from the three records and tested which of its numbers the data decide. A patch below is a group of destroyed buildings, each linked to another by a set distance.

How we got to the working rule

The question, each step we took to answer it, and the proposal it led to. The numbers are the current ones, on the fire outline the paper now uses.

  1. 1
    12 October 2026 The question
    Cat Fong and the project lead asked: “Is there a quantification for urban conflagration?” — a way to say, from a map of destroyed buildings, which wildfires turned into town fires that spread from building to building. We started from a working rule first used on 8 October: at least 50 destroyed buildings in one connected patch, each within 30 m of the next.
  2. 2
    12 October Which fires reach that line?
    The best single predictor was the largest block of closely spaced buildings the fire reached: no fire whose largest block held 89 buildings or fewer reached the line (Our 2002–26 record: 0 of 714 fires; 10 of 25 above it). The chance rose steeply but smoothly, with no step.
  3. 3
    13 October Is town fire a separate kind of fire?
    Six other ways of describing the loss (share of destroyed buildings with a destroyed neighbour, loss per square kilometre, how deep the loss went into town, and others) all set these fires apart, but as one continuous spread, not a separate class.
  4. 4
    13 October Do the data draw their own line?
    No natural size: the largest patch thins out smoothly from fire to fire. No single natural distance: destroyed buildings cluster more than chance over about 20–50 m between building centres. Published work gives building-to-building ignition distances (most often 9.1–18 m wall to wall) but no number that defines an urban conflagration.
  5. 5
    13 October Is another definition better?
    We scored the working rule against 5 alternatives on how well each matches published accounts of named fires and how stable its list of fires is. None did better; the working rule is a knife-edge choice (nudging either number swaps borderline fires in or out).
  6. 6
    13–14 October A part of a fire, not the whole fire
    Patches, not fires, are the unit: a fire can hold none, one or several urban conflagrations. Fires with one that hold two or more: Carlson 2002–22 4 of 8; Our 2002–26 record 6 of 10; CAL FIRE DINS 2013–25 5 of 7. Linking houses through continuous tree canopy, as well as by distance, catches wooded-town fires the house rule misses.
  7. 7
    15 October A check on fires held out from the start
    On 2016–2022 fires kept out of all of this work, none of the 66 with a block of 89 or fewer became an urban conflagration. It is a weak check: none of the held-out fires became one at all.
What we propose. Call a patch of at least 50 destroyed buildings, each within 30 m centre to centre (about 15 m wall to wall for typical houses) of another in the patch, an urban conflagration, and say plainly that 50 and 30 m are a stated convention, not a line the data draw. A fire can hold none, one or several. Report 50 m links as the sensitivity (in Our 2002–26 record they count 24 fires instead of 10), and keep the fires counted under every nearby rule apart from the borderline ones.

Two real fires, four link distances

In Tubbs 2017 fire spread house to house through Santa Rosa's Coffey Park; Chimney Tops 2 2016 destroyed about as many buildings in and around Gatlinburg, over steep, wooded hills. Switch the link distance. At 30 m, Tubbs passes the 50-building line (143) and Gatlinburg does not (16), and even Coffey Park, which burned almost completely, splits into many patches. At 50 m Tubbs joins into one patch of 1,250; at 100 m Gatlinburg's largest patch reaches 500. Is there a natural size? No: the largest patch thins out smoothly from fire to fire

Each line shows, for one record, the share of fires whose largest patch of destroyed buildings is at least a given size. If urban conflagrations were a separate kind of fire, the lines would drop and then flatten, leaving a gap between ordinary fires and town fires. They don't: patch sizes thin out smoothly from 1 building to the largest, 378. A formal test for a second peak found none at any distance from 5 to 100 m in any record. The 50-building line sits on a smooth slope; it is a convention.Complementary CDF of the largest destroyed chain at 30 m over fires with ≥ 10 destroyed. Silverman critical-bandwidth test (2,000 smoothed bootstraps) on log10 of the largest destroyed chain, 10 link distances × 3 records, Holm-adjusted p ≥ 1.00 everywhere (smallest raw p 0.113). Fisher–Jenks 2-class break at 30 m: 8 [5–11], 8 [5–11], 8 [5–16] buildings (bootstrap ranges span more than a factor of 2). Gaussian mixtures prefer 2 components at L ≥ 20 m, but on skewed data that is expected and is not separation.

Destroyed buildings cluster more than chance, building up between about 20 and 50 m

For each fire we redrew the same number of destroyed buildings at random among the fire's own buildings and compared the largest patch with the real one. Real patches are bigger than chance at every distance above 5 m. Half of the extra clustering is reached by 20 m between centres and nearly all of it by 30–50 m; beyond that it adds little. So destroyed buildings hang together more than chance over roughly 20–50 m, and 30 m sits inside that range; fire by fire, the distance of strongest clustering varies by more than a factor of two, so the data give a range, not one number.Contagion ratio = largest destroyed chain at L / mean of 50 random-labelling draws, median over fires with ≥ 20 destroyed, fire-bootstrap 95% CI. Pre-registered bar for a natural linkage distance (per-fire IQR within a factor of 2 and medians within ±25% in all three records) not met by either the per-fire jump or the per-fire peak; the half-way and levelling-off distances are exploratory.

3 · When a wildfire becomes a town fire

With the definition in hand: when can a town fire happen, and how does it spread once it does? A block below is a group of buildings that stood before the fire, each within 35 m of another.

No fire became an urban conflagration below a block of 90 closely spaced buildings, but almost none below could have

Group each fire's buildings that stood before it into blocks (houses whose centres are within 35 m of each other). No fire whose largest block held 89 buildings or fewer became an urban conflagration: 0 of 338 in Carlson, 0 of 714 in our record and 0 of 429 in CAL FIRE's inspections. Above the line it happened in 35–44% of fires. But when we tested it, almost no fire just below the line could have made one: of the 16, 18 and 13 fires with blocks of 50–89, only 2, 2 and 3 had both 50 destroyed buildings and 50 buildings close enough to chain. What it suggests: the line marks the smallest town that can hold an urban conflagration under the 30 m rule, not a tipping point in how fires behave (tested here).Condition 1 on the paper outline (MTBS + 100 m), all fires with ≥ 1 exposed building (361, 739, 445 fires; 8, 10, 7 events). Cut 89 = two-rate split on log10(1 + largest exposed 35 m component). Part of the line is built in: a 30 m destroyed patch of ≥ 50 must lie inside a block of ≥ 50, so the evidence for 89 is the zero among blocks of 50–89, and of those only 2 / 2 / 3 had ≥ 50 destroyed and a ≥ 50 group at 30 m (capacity test; null models that keep each fire's losses give a 61–86 % chance of none below anyway; the line moves with the 30 m chain distance). Exact binomial intervals. Held-out check, 2016–22 back-cast: 0 of 66 at or below 89 (weak: no held-out fire reached 50 at 30 m).

How this panel was checked
  • All three full records, on the paper's fire outline, all fires with at least one building in reach.
  • Exact intervals: with so few fires near the line the true rate just below it could be a few per cent, not zero.

Every urban conflagration burned in a recognised wind event, but so did most big blocks that did not

A fire counts as a recognised wind event when the offshore pressure push was among the rarest 5 % of hours, or a High Wind or Extreme Wind Warning or Wind Advisory was in effect while the town burned. In our 2002–26 record, 10 of the 10 fires that became urban conflagrations were recognised wind events, and so were 14 of the 15 whose big block did not; Carlson 2002–22: 8 of 8 vs 14 of 15; CAL FIRE DINS 2013–25: 7 of 7 vs 6 of 9. What it suggests: a wind event went with every urban conflagration, but it does not single them out: most big blocks that did not become one burned in a wind event too. Hover a published account for its source.

Offshore pairs (ERA5 MSLP at airport cells): LAX−DAG / LAX−TPH (CA < 35.5°N), SFO−WMC / SFO−RNO (CA ≥ 35.5°N), PDX−DLS (OR, WA); min over burn window, percentile among all hours 1991–2020; strong ≤ 1 %, moderate ≤ 5 %. Warnings: IEM json/vtec_events_bypoint.py at the town point (public and fire-weather zones), FW.W, HW.W, EW.W, WI.Y overlapping the burn window; archive from 2005-10-01. No historical Santa Ana Wildfire Threat Index archive is public; the Abatzoglou et al. 2023 catalogue of downslope-wind fires is cited as context, its data were not reachable.

How this panel was checked
  • The event rule was fixed before looking (pre-registered): rarest 5 % offshore push, or a High Wind / Extreme Wind Warning or Wind Advisory; Red Flag alone does not count.
  • Pressure from one weather map (ERA5) for every year, so 2003 and 2025 are judged the same way.
  • Fires before the warning archive are marked 'unknown', never 'no'.
  • Published accounts were checked on 2026-10-14: each DOI fetched from Crossref and the abstract or report read; two were corrected (Camp: the source confirms a downslope windstorm but not the Jarbo Gap detail; Chimney Tops 2: a mountain-wave event, not downslope), and one (Keeley et al. 2004) was replaced for the 2003 fires because its readable abstract does not mention wind. They are context and do not feed the rule.

Full analysis: Trees, fences and wind in urban conflagrations. Tested further on Testing three findings: the rule could have failed (at the same towns and season it flags about one ordinary day in five), and Waldo Canyon 2012, an urban conflagration outside our three records, burned with no recognised wind event.

House to house: at most about a third of losses were lit by a burning neighbour, about twice as many where the block is big

From each fire's final map of destroyed and surviving buildings we estimated how many buildings the wildfire alone would not have destroyed: they were lost because a building near them burned. Across the three records that is 28–39% of all destroyed buildings, and the share is higher where the block is big: about 45–57% in the typical fire above the 89-building line against 20–28% below it. What it suggests: a large block matters because it lets fire jump from house to house. The level is an upper bound and depends on how gradual we let the wildfire's own advance be (20–47% across the settings we tried); the gap between big and small blocks holds in every record.Final-outcome spread model with a smooth background (the wildfire's push, from the fire's broad loss map, scale 200 m) plus an exponential building-to-building kernel; snapshot bias corrected by simulation on each fire's own buildings (approximate Bayesian computation). Fires with ≥ 50 destroyed: 135, 155, 51 fires; pooled share 36% [30, 42], 39% [31, 47], 28% [19, 38]. A no-spread trap test partly fooled the estimator, so shares are upper bounds. How this panel was checked
  • All three full records, fires with at least 50 destroyed buildings, on the paper's fire outline.

Cat Fong's fitted house-to-house push would have to be about 34 times stronger for fire to keep itself going

Cat's contagion model says each burning building nearby slightly raises a building's chance of burning (fitted push β ≈ 0.035, fading over about 12.5 m). Put on the real web of buildings, that push is far too weak for fire to keep going from house to house on its own: it would have to be about 34 times stronger in the median fire, and 9 times in Tubbs 2017, 13 times in Camp 2018, 21 times in Marshall 2021, 12 times in Eaton 2025, 21 times in Lahaina 2023 even in the most tightly packed part of the big urban fires. So urban conflagrations need the wildfire's help (wind, embers, many ignitions at once); house-to-house spread adds to the loss, as the section above estimates, but does not drive it alone.Cat's model as a network: P_ij = 1 − exp(−β K_ij), K = exp(−d/12.5 m), pairs ≤ 60 m, built on each 30 m group of standing buildings. A self-sustaining outbreak needs the spectral radius ρ(P) > 1 (Wang et al. 2003; Newman 2002). Max ρ(P) at β = 0.035 over all fires: 0.20 / 0.20 / 0.14 (three records). β_crit = 1/ρ(K) for each fire's most tightly packed 30 m group; median over 353 / 440 / 110 fires with ≥ 10 destroyed. Cat's β and λ were fitted to the residual distance-response in Carlson 2013–22 after adjusting for the wildfire (Fong 2026 briefing).

Full analysis: Urban conflagrations as networks.

Inside a burning town, losses do not lean downwind

For every destroyed building we looked at its neighbours within 60 m and asked whether those downwind of it were lost more often than those upwind. They were not: in our 2002–26 record (159 fires, each counted once) neighbours downwind were lost 73.4 % of the time and neighbours upwind 74.0 %, and Carlson 2002–22 and CAL FIRE DINS 2013–25 agree. Any downwind lean is at most about 2 points in every record, well below the 12 points IBHS reported for Eaton and Palisades with a different measure. What it suggests: wind carries fire into a town, but once inside it does not pick which neighbour of a lost house burns next.

Statistic (pre-registered primary): mean over fires of p_down − p_up, where p is the share destroyed among ordered pairs (destroyed A → any B, centres ≤ 60 m) with B's bearing from A within ±45° of the downwind direction (vector-mean 10 m wind over the town's satellite-timed burn window ± 3 h; CONUS404 4 km to Sep 2024, RTMA 2.5 km after). Carlson −0.51 (−2.23 to +1.15), ours −0.54 (−2.04 to +1.07), CAL FIRE −0.58 (−2.85 to +1.84); 2,000 fire-bootstrap draws; rotated-wind p 0.59 / 0.54 / 0.67. Pre-registered verdict: can't tell (same sign, bars not met): no record meets the downwind or upwind bar, and the ±2-point equivalence bar is narrowly missed on the upwind side (lower bounds −2.2 / −2.0 / −2.9). Destroyed–destroyed pairs are symmetric (each counts once downwind and once upwind: 97,567 pairs each way in our record), so the lean is carried only by where the surviving neighbours sit. Bearings on true north (building points converted from the national grid before any angle).

How this panel was checked
  • Pre-registered before any number was computed; one recorded amendment added two checks (observation-based map only; fires where two maps agree) after the main run showed the 4 km map's direction was off for Tubbs and Marshall. Neither changes the answer.
  • Like for like: same statistic, distance (60 m), sectors and fire rule in all three full records, side by side. Fires without a town wind reading (fewer than 100 buildings nearby) are left out: our record 102 fires holding 1,705 destroyed buildings, CAL FIRE 24 incidents holding 583.
  • Denominators: building pairs within 60 m of a destroyed building, by sector; every share in the hovers names its pairs. Each fire counts once in the headline; the all-pairs version (big fires weigh more) and the version without the largest fire (Camp) are in the hovers and give the same answer.
  • Uncertainty from the independent unit: fires resampled 2,000 times; the rotated wind check keeps each town's real loss map and layout fixed and only turns the wind, so street and valley directions cannot create a false lean.
  • Town layout: a second measure compares the direction of lines between lost buildings with the direction of lines between all buildings in the town before the fire. No record shows lost pairs lining up with the wind more than the layout does.
  • Wind direction is uncertain: burn-window directions from the 4 km simulation (CONUS404) are within 45° of the coarse global map (ERA5) for 271 of 327 fires; the two observation-based maps (HRRR, RTMA) agree for 228 of 243. Every alternative wind source gives the same answer (checks table).
  • The side the fire came from gives a lean as small as the wind's, so this test cannot separate the two; neither shows a lean.
  • Claims match the evidence: 'no downwind lean shown', with ranges that exclude a downwind lean above about 1–2 points depending on record; an upwind lean of up to about 3 points cannot be ruled out. This does not contradict IBHS (damaged vs destroyed, 3 m wall gaps vs 60 m centres, two fires); their exact measure needs footprints and wall-to-wall gaps.
  • Fire weather is a description only here; it is never part of a definition or a model input.

Full analysis: Trees, fences and wind in urban conflagrations.

4 · What puts a building at risk inside a fire

Two comparisons inside fires: crowded against sparse buildings, and mobile homes against houses in the same fire.

Urban conflagrations lean their losses toward the most crowded buildings, but many other fires do too

Each line is one fire. Sort the buildings the fire reached from the most isolated (fewest neighbours within 100 m) to the most crowded and add up as you go: the line shows how much of the fire's losses had been reached at each step. A line on the dashed diagonal means losses fell evenly on sparse and crowded buildings; a line that sags below it means they piled up at the crowded end. In our 2002–26 record all 10 urban conflagrations are drawn (orange) with the 145 other fires that destroyed 50 or more (blue). A typical urban conflagration had 25% of its losses in its most crowded fifth of buildings, against 17% for other big fires and 14% for fires with 10–49 destroyed (20% would mean losses simply follow the buildings). What it suggests: urban conflagrations do lean to the crowded end, but many other fires look the same, and some urban conflagrations (Woolsey, Glass) do not lean at all. How much more often are mobile homes destroyed than houses in the same fire?

In the same fire, a mobile home is destroyed about 1.2 times as often as a single-family home in the CAL FIRE inspections (1.15–1.41; odds 2.4×), 1.4× in Carlson (1.11–2.05) and 1.4× in our record (1.12–1.90). The ratio looks small because in the inspected areas 51% of single-family homes were destroyed too. At the same building size the CAL FIRE gap nearly closes (1.02× (0.95–1.33)). 5 · What only the extended record can show

Two results that need what we added to Carlson's record: fires that destroyed few or no buildings, and an inventory of what stood before each fire.

Studying only fires known to have destroyed buildings makes a typical fire look 2 to 3 times as destructive

Most loss studies, Carlson's included, start from fires already known to have destroyed buildings. Our model lets us score every 2023–25 fire that reached at least 25 buildings, including fires nobody reported. In that full set a typical fire destroyed 9% of the buildings it reached; picking fires by reported loss doubles that (×1.9), and keeping only fires with 10 or more destroyed triples it (×3.0). What it suggests: per-fire destruction rates from loss-selected samples describe bad fires, not fires in general. The share of fires that destroyed nothing is uncertain: 44% by the model's calls, 75% after allowing for its false alarms.Unselected WFIGS 2023–25 frame, ≥ 25 Overture buildings within 100 m, 383 fires scored; per-fire mean D/N (Direct zone, first call). How this panel was checked
  • Two sources: Carlson 2002–22 for 2002–2022, CAL FIRE DINS 2013–25 (its 2023–2025 inspections) for 2023–2025 (Carlson stops in 2022).

Full analysis: Our wildfire building-loss model in Canada and Mexico.

Leads we have not chased (ideas welcome)

  • Official zeros that are not zero. Tested: about 1 in 13 fires that destroyed 10 or more buildings reads 0 or is missing in the national reports, but they hold only a few percent of destroyed buildings; the 2023–25 national shortfall is roughly 1–8%, mostly in the South (Testing three findings).
  • Today's building maps forget past losses (last panel). Anyone measuring exposure from a current map undercounts the buildings old fires destroyed. How much does that bias published risk models?
  • Why does wind not pick the next house? Wind drives fires into towns, yet losses do not lean downwind house to house. Embers arriving from far upwind, or fire moving through yards, could both explain it.
  • Where it could happen next. We mapped every block big enough, within reach of wildland: the national map.
  • Outside the U.S. No fire below the line became an urban conflagration in ten other countries either, though our model is less reliable there and far fewer fires above the line did: Urban conflagrations outside the U.S.. What the literature says: How researchers think about urban conflagrations.
